items.title: [Editorial] Multiple sclerosis: beyond controlling relapses
items.summary: Few neurological diseases have seen a transformation in diagnosis and treatment as remarkable as multiple sclerosis. A chronic, heterogeneous autoimmune condition, it typically begins in early adulthood and affects over 3 million people, with women roughly three times more likely to be affected than men. Characterised by inflammation, demyelination, axonal injury, and neuronal loss, multiple sclerosis can cause relapses and gradual accumulation of disability. Three decades ago, treatment options were few and far between; today, more than 20 disease-modifying therapies are available.

items.title: [Perspectives] What do artists know?
items.summary: Until the day my newborn son died, I worked as an artist. I spent each day in the studio making drawings and films, over 15 years preparing work for exhibitions, commissions, and eventually a doctorate in fine art. After he died (in my arms, peacefully, not unexpectedly), I directed everything I had learned as an artist into writing the story of his birth and death. As it turned out, over those years in the studio I had developed aptitudes well matched to drawing meaning from experience too adverse to bear.

items.title: [Correspondence] Defining success in kidney xenotransplantation
items.summary: Leonardo V Riella and colleagues report the first successful transition from porcine kidney xenotransplantation to allotransplantation.1 The possibility of this bridge raises important questions about its purpose and how its success should be defined—traditionally by graft survival.2 Xenotransplantation could serve different purposes, including reducing time on dialysis for patients waiting for an allograft, decreasing waiting-list mortality, or providing an alternative for patients unlikely to receive an allograft.

items.title: General anaesthesia rates for Caesarean delivery: a quality metric or a marker of system capacity?
items.summary: General anaesthesia for Caesarean delivery is increasingly used as a quality indicator, but general anaesthesia rates alone are not measures of quality. The multinational anaesthesia practice for Caesarean delivery snapshot study demonstrates variation in general anaesthesia use across European centres, emphasising the need to interpret these rates within the systems in which anaesthetic decisions occur. We propose an interpretation framework based on three domains: access to appropriate neuraxial care, reliability of neuraxial techniques and rescue pathways, and patient experience.

items.title: A call for post-implementation evaluation of the 2025 UK neurological death criteria in practice

Testing rates were declining before the revised Code, precluding simple attribution of that decline to its introduction. items.title: Impact of high versus low fraction of inspired oxygen for anaesthetic washout and extubation on postoperative pulmonary atelectasis formation and oxygenation: defining peri-extubation oxygen exposure before identifying the optimal inspired fraction. Comment on Br J Anaesth 2026; 137: 591–600
items.summary: We read with interest the randomised controlled trial by Paschold and colleagues1 evaluating fraction of inspired oxygen (Fio2) values of 1.0, 0.7, or 0.4 during anaesthetic washout and tracheal extubation. The study provides useful physiological evidence that avoiding pure oxygen can reduce the immediate postextubation loss of end-expiratory lung volume (EELV) and preserve a more dorsal distribution of ventilation. However, calling an Fio2 of 0.7 the optimal strategy could be premature because several aspects of peri-extubation oxygen exposure and respiratory status were not fully defined.
